newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy unveils budget, promises welfare reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy unveils budget, promises welfare reform.

text.p: The Italian government approved a mini-budget on Thursday, largely based on tax and accountancy changes, which Prime Minister Romano Prodi said would ensure Italy becomes a founder member of the single European currency.
The package, designed to raise 15.5 trillion lire ($9.2 billion) in 1997, was roundly condemned by the opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance bloc as a damaging collection of stopgap measures.

But Prodi told reporters that the corrective budget would benefit state accounts over the next three years and promised to start negotiations with unions and coalition allies on reform of the welfare state next month.
"The single currency is close at hand and with this budget we have overcome the scepticism of those who did not believe in us," Prodi said. "Today we have closed a chapter."
The government said it would raise six trillion lire from the mini-budget by forcing companies to pay tax advances on their huge pools of severance payment funds.

A further 4.2 trillion lire will come from changing tax payment mechanisms, while the rest of the cash will be brought in by ministerial spending cuts and by imposing a temporary block on state workers drawing early retirement handouts.
"This will weigh on (public) finances in the years to come. It's a real timebomb," said Antonio Marzano, a leading figure in former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia party.
Pierferdinando Casini, head of the centrist CCD party was equally damning: "It is worse than all our expectations."

The package has to be approved by parliament, with the government enjoying a majority in the upper house but relying in the lower house on hard-left allies Communist Refoundation who hold the balance of power and back the measures.

Prodi said the latest round of belt tightening would cut the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product from 6.7 percent in 1996, and guarantee Italy a place on the starting blocks for the launch of the single currency in 1999.
Newspapers, which were leaked partial details of the budget for their Thursday editions, were less certain.

"The Germans will renounce the single currency rather than share it with a country that might artificially get its deficit to the three percent level but has not found the political consensus needed to resolve long-term problems..." Corriere della Sera said in a front page editorial.
Financial markets were little moved as full news of the budget package emerged.
"There is relief that the coalition was at least able to agree on the budget but disappointment that the content wasn't more meaty," said one bond trader, based in London.

Economists hope the meat will come with a reform of social spending, especially the generous state pension system, arguing that this is the only way to secure lasting peace for Italy's heavily indebted economy.

Prodi said an eventual reform will be enshrined in the 1998 budget, which has to be approved by parliament before the end of this year, but he faces an uphill battle trying to win any meaningful deal from his disparate coalition.
"I do not have the backing of anyone, there is agreement on opening the negotiations, the contents have to be defined, it will be a hard and tough discussion," he admitted on Thursday.
One of the biggest opponents to cuts in the welfare state is Communist Refoundation. "Now we face the mother of all problems -- social spending," Bertinotti said on Thursday.
